Kisvarda Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Kisvárda, Hungary

Not demolished. Kisvárda's Jewish cemetery is dated by its oldest tombstone to 1855, though other sources place its founding as early as 1824. Jews first appear in local records in 1730, settling under a special permit from Count Eszterházy; the community organized formally in 1796, building its first synagogue and school by 1801, and gained independence from Nagykálló's jurisdiction in 1844. From 1885, Kisvárda became the hub for numerous smaller surrounding Jewish communities. Jews played an outsized economic role locally - in retail, estate management, agricultural warehousing, food-industry manufacturing, and banking - and by 1900 the community's school served 370 students alongside a large yeshiva. A grand new synagogue opened in 1901. Hungary's 1938 antisemitic laws stripped Jewish bank owners and civil servants of their positions; by April 1944, close to 7,000 Jews from Kisvárda and surrounding areas were crowded into its ghetto before deportation to Auschwitz that May. About 800 survivors returned after the war, but most emigrated to Israel or the US following the 1956 uprising. The Great Synagogue was sold to the city council in 1975 and has served as a museum since 1983. This cemetery's newest tombstones date to 1983.
